cells.tense: Right now what leans on you holds firm, and you are still in the room while it does.
cells.ask: Tell one person who shares the load what bearing it has been like — facts, not a report card. Let what they hand back land without fixing it.
cells.core:
Things lean on you and they hold. You're not white-knuckling it and you're not collapsing under it either. The people near you feel that steadiness, and they rest on it more than you'd guess.

The pull toward what you actually want is here too. It's orientation, not fantasy — you know which direction is yours, and when you stay in touch with that while you bear the weight, the bearing stays clean. The next thing this balance is free to feed is being with somebody inside it: not fusing, not managing them, just letting their weight and yours share a room. That's the growth, and it costs something. You can't be the only one who knows what this costs.
cells.sheetLine: You bear it and stay in the room with people.
cells.place: inside the pull toward what you genuinely want

cells.tense: You are bracing for a load that hasn't arrived yet, gripping harder than this moment requires.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you're most braced about. Do the next right action on it, once, then leave it for a day without checking.
cells.core:
You're bracing ahead of the moment. Whatever's coming next week, next month, next year — you've already taken its shape and started bearing it. Strength that belongs to today is being spent on loads that haven't landed.

When the grip runs past what the moment needs, it starts to feel like the only thing keeping everything together. It isn't. What you actually want should orient how you carry this, not the fear of what you're braced against. Fairness is the way through: give this moment the weight it really has, no more. Ease the grip on what hasn't arrived and what's yours comes back to the present. What it costs is the belief that gripping harder is what keeps you safe.
cells.sheetLine: You're braced against a load nobody handed you.
cells.place: inside the pull toward what you genuinely want

cells.tense: Holding anything has felt too risky for a while, and you have stayed out from under it.
cells.ask: Let one thing go that's already finished. Say out loud, 'that's done,' and mean it. Don't pick up the next weight to replace it.
cells.core:
You've stopped letting things rest on you. Whatever asked to be borne, you've kept your hands off it, and the spot where that decision got made is where you still live. Nothing leans on you now, and nothing falls.

The pull toward what you actually want is still here. It hasn't gone anywhere, and it doesn't require you to be able to bear everything — knowing your direction isn't the same as enduring. What's drained is the bearing itself, and forcing it back won't work. Letting something go because it's completed, not because you failed — that's the way in. When that loosens, the aspiration has a spine to sit in.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped letting anything rest on you.

cells.tense: You are already bearing more than you claim, and the pull that steers you runs without your name on it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you have held steady for longer than a month. Say what it has cost and what it has made possible. Then say it was yours.
cells.core:
You bear more than you give yourself credit for. It doesn't show up in your account of yourself — you'd call it keeping it together, or just getting through. But people near you lean on that steadiness and feel it working. The pull toward what you actually want is running under it too, steering more than you own.

The doing is live. Owning it isn't. When what you've been bearing goes unclaimed, it runs on default and doesn't get fed. The simpler earlier form of the same line is where the credit returns: not 'I held everything,' just 'I held that, and that was mine.' Radiance comes from what was actually cultivated reaching completion — not from performance, from seeing what was already done and saying so.
cells.sheetLine: You're already bearing it. You just haven't claimed it.
cells.place: inside the pull toward what you genuinely want

attempts.check: The record doesn't say the person has lost a specific past collapse or carries a particular history — so Too Little must locate the past-anchor without naming what happened, who, how long, or what it cost. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not gripping anything, I just plan ahead' — so the Too Much cell must describe the bracing in a way they can recognize in a moment without being told their motive. The asks survive a wrong read because each one is a small doable act that teaches something about what is actually being held, not a fix for a condition. The sentence that serves me more than them is any variant of 'you already know which star' — it sounds like praise and puts a claim in their mouth.
